changes.after: Kotlin chooses an extension function from the receiver's known type at compile time.

before: fun Base.label() declares an extension with Base as receiver. It does not add an overridable member to Base or gain access to its private members.

When multiple extensions have the same name, selection uses the receiver’s compile-time type. A derived object held in a Base variable therefore uses the Base extension. Actual overridable members still dispatch dynamically; a matching member also takes priority over an extension.

The no-argument label call below has two different declared receiver types. The Base receiver returns "base" even though it holds a Detail object; the Detail receiver returns "detail". Neither extension overrides the other.
```kotlin
open class Base
class Detail : Base()
fun Base.label(): String = "base"
fun Detail.label(): String = "detail"
fun main() {
    val broad: Base = Detail()
    val narrow: Detail = Detail()
    println(broad.label())
    println(narrow.label())
}
```
Expected output: base; detail.

after: An extension function can be called with dot notation without being added inside the class. In `fun Base.label()`, Base is the receiver type. This extension does not gain access to the class's private details.

Kotlin chooses between these extensions using the type known at the call site when it compiles the code. This is called static resolution. It does not choose by the actual object's child class, as an overridden member function would.

Follow the example one line at a time.
```kotlin
open class Base
class Detail : Base()
fun Base.label(): String = "base"
fun Detail.label(): String = "detail"
fun main() {
    val item: Base = Detail()
    println(item.label())
}
```
The screen shows `base`. The object is a Detail, but item is declared as Base. That declared type selects the Base extension.
A matching function defined inside the class takes priority over an extension. Two extensions with the same name do not override each other.
